# Midterm Project: PM2.5 and Congestion Pricing

New York City began charging most vehicles entering the Congestion Relief
Zone (CRZ) on January 5, 2025. The CRZ covers Manhattan's local streets and
avenues south of and including 60th Street, with exemptions for the FDR Drive,
West Side Highway/Route 9A, and connections from the Hugh L. Carey Tunnel to
West Street [@mta2024crz]. Did the odds of a high-PM2.5 day at CRZ
monitors change after the policy began, accounting for regional background
conditions? We define a high day relative to the pre-policy CRZ data; this is
a study-specific threshold, not a health standard.

This project builds on a published analysis of congestion pricing and air
quality [@fraser2025first] and extends its data through August 2026. Fraser et
al. analyze continuous daily PM2.5 using prediction-based counterfactuals; the
high-day outcome and segmented logistic model here are a separate course
analysis, not the paper's model. The analysis can show whether measurements
changed around the policy date. It cannot, by itself, show that
the toll caused a change. Weather, wildfire smoke, traffic, monitor operations,
and other events can affect PM2.5 at the same time. Your report must separate
the model's estimated association from a causal conclusion.

Use Python for this project. There is no restriction on which Python packages
you use. A grammar-of-graphics library such as `plotnine` is welcome.
Document the packages needed to reproduce your report.
Include executable Python code that reads the supplied data from a local
`data/` folder, documents each cleaning choice, and produces the tables and
figures you discuss.

Two ZIP files are provided, covering June 1, 2023, through
August 31, 2026: [NYCCAS data](data/nyccas.zip) and
[AirNow data](data/airnow.zip). Each ZIP contains one hourly CSV file. Keep
both ZIPs in a local `data/` folder next to your report. You may read the
CSV files directly from the ZIPs or extract them first. Do not include the
data files in your submission.

- `nyccas.csv` contains readings from six NYCCAS monitors inside the
  CRZ, with location and site information.
- `airnow.csv` contains readings from four regional AirNow
  monitors used to estimate background PM2.5: Flemington, Rutgers University,
  Chester, and Paterson.

NYCCAS records are hourly averages, in micrograms per cubic meter, and the
`ObservationTimeUTC` field explicitly identifies UTC. AirNow’s `datetime`
field has no timezone offset in the CSV, but the AirNow hourly data
specification reports observation times in GMT (UTC). In both files, a
timestamp marks the beginning of its hour. The two files use different column
names and formats. Read the source descriptions and inspect the files before
deciding how to clean and combine them. AirNow may contain special or invalid
concentration codes; determine how to handle them from the values and
documentation. Do not treat a missing monitor reading as zero.

The data come from the NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS) archive
[@nyccasarchive] and the AirNow API [@airnowapi]. The AirNow hourly data
specification documents its GMT timestamp convention [@airnowhourly].
NYCCAS readings are preliminary and its historical files can be revised. The
accompanying [data README](data/README.md) explains which source snapshots
contribute to each period and documents NYCCAS correction changes and records
removed after sensor problems. Cite both data sources in
your report.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-pm25-clean}
Inspect and clean the hourly source files.

a. Describe the observational unit, time field and time zone, monitor key,
   PM2.5 value field, and units in each file.
b. Standardize the needed column names and parse timestamps as UTC. Check
   null values, duplicate monitor-hour records, and gaps between each
   monitor's first and last observations. Report missing hours by monitor
   and identify one month with a notable gap. Distinguish absent hours from
   null cells and time before a monitor began reporting.
c. Investigate unusual AirNow values, including negative codes. Identify
   codes that cannot be valid concentrations, document the exclusion rule,
   and keep the original files unchanged.
d. Apply the paper's strict range, $0 < PM_{2.5} < 25.5$ µg/m³, after
   removing invalid codes. Report retained and excluded counts. Explain
   which valid zeros and high readings this rule removes and why some high
   readings could be real events.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-daily}
Create daily data and merge the sources.

a. Calculate daily maxima separately for each NYCCAS and AirNow monitor.
   Average the available AirNow monitor maxima for each date and report how
   many monitors contribute to each background estimate.
b. Create dates from the UTC timestamps. Show one example hour whose
   New York local calendar date differs from its UTC date, and explain why
   the chosen date convention matters for a daily maximum.
c. Join date-level background estimates to NYCCAS monitor-days. Report row
   counts before and after the join, validate its cardinality, and explain
   how dates without background measurements are handled. Do not join the
   hourly files directly or replace missing measurements with zero.
d. Create a policy indicator that switches on January 5, 2025, and a variable
   counting days since that date. Retain January 2025 and explain how the
   intervention date determines these variables.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-eda}
Explore and visualize the hourly and daily measurements.

a. Make a faceted plot of CRZ monitor daily maxima by month, with separate
   weekday panels. Describe one seasonal pattern and one weekday comparison.
   Explain what the facets make easier to see.
b. Plot the daily regional background series alongside the CRZ series.
   Compare the CRZ-minus-background difference before and after the policy
   date and explain why this raw contrast is descriptive.
c. Summarize how many AirNow monitors contribute to each daily background
   estimate and how many CRZ sites contribute over time. Explain why missing
   measurements are not zero-valued measurements.
d. Plot the daily CRZ-minus-background PM2.5 distributions before and
   after January 5, 2025. Compare their medians and spreads. Use a two-sided
   Mann–Whitney U test to compare the distributions: state the hypotheses,
   report both sample sizes, the test statistic and $p$-value, and interpret
   the result at the 0.05 level. Explain the test's independence assumption
   and why seasonality and nearby-day dependence limit its interpretation.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-model}
Model high-PM2.5 days and interpret the results.

For each UTC date, average the available CRZ monitor-specific daily
maxima. Define a high day as a CRZ daily mean above its pre-policy 75th
percentile. This study-specific cutoff is not a health standard.

Fit a segmented logistic model with time in years from the study start
($t$), an indicator for January 5, 2025, onward ($T_t$), years since that
date set to zero beforehand ($D_t$), and daily AirNow background. Fraser et
al. use square-rooted background; justify your chosen form. Other covariates,
such as month or day type, are your choice. A general model is

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(H_t=1)}{1-P(H_t=1)}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 T_t + \beta_3 D_t + g(X_t),
$$

where $H_t$ marks a high day and $g(X_t)$ contains AirNow background and
any other covariates. The coefficients $\beta_2$ and $\beta_3$ describe
the immediate level change and the change in yearly trend, respectively.

a. Calculate the high-day cutoff and indicator. Report high and non-high
   day counts, the number of dates, and CRZ monitor coverage.
b. Fit the segmented logistic model. Report and interpret the intervention
   level-change and trend-change odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals.
   Explain your AirNow background term and any other covariates.
c. Plot observed high days and fitted probabilities over time. Describe the
   pre-policy and post-policy patterns and whether the fitted change is an
   immediate shift, a trend change, or both.
d. Conclude by answering the research question. Use the residual pattern,
   dependence between nearby days, regional background, and possible
   confounding to explain how far the result supports a causal claim.
:::

**Submission.**
Organize the report around these four steps. Include the Python code that
produces every reported result, and explain each cleaning and modeling choice.
Use ideas from chapters 1–9 of the
[course book](https://statds.github.io/ids-book/): reproducible projects,
data checks, preparation, EDA, visualization, and logistic-model interpretation.

Submit an independently written Quarto report to the Classroom 50 assignment.
Include your source code, selected tables and figures, cleaning decisions,
model output, and interpretation. Your report must run when the supplied ZIP
files are placed in the expected local `data/` folder. Do not submit the raw
or cleaned data files.
